CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Continue intensive negotiations toward a deal, accepting pragmatic concessions on IP protection and market access while holding firm on sovereignty over the enforcement mechanism. Push for a Trump-Xi summit to finalize a deal that preserves China's core industrial policy space. Do not escalate or retaliate at this stage — the current trajectory favors China.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat score of +0.3 reflects a moderate, non-existential threat. The US has imposed tariffs on ~$250B of Chinese exports (Lists 1-3, timeline entries June-Sept 2018) and is demanding structural reforms on IP, forced technology transfer, subsidies, and market access that would constrain China's development model. The Huawei CFO arrest (Dec 1, 2018) and subsequent DOJ indictments (Jan 28, 2019) signal a broader technology containment strategy. However, the threat is tempered by several factors: (1) China's economy is proving resilient — Q1 2019 GDP beat expectations at 6.4%, March industrial production surged 8.5% YoY (strongest since July 2014), and retail sales grew 8.7%, all aided by massive stimulus (8.2 trillion yuan in Q1 credit); (2) negotiations are genuinely progressing — both sides report progress on text across six areas, and as of April 10, Mnuchin confirmed an enforcement mechanism is 'basically' agreed including bilateral enforcement offices; (3) China has already made 'unprecedented proposals' on forced technology transfer (US officials, March 28), showing willingness to move on substance.

The action score of +0.15 (negotiate) reflects the judgment that China's best path is continued engagement rather than escalation or capitulation. Escalation would be counterproductive: the US has bipartisan domestic support for toughness on China, and further retaliation would risk expanding tariffs to remaining Chinese exports while the stimulus cushion has limits. But maximal concession is also wrong — the US demands on enforcement mechanisms risk sovereignty (Lighthizer seeking unilateral reimposition rights), and fully dismantling state support for strategic industries would undermine Made in China 2025. The smart play is to concede on areas where China's new Foreign Investment Law already moves in the same direction (IP protection, voluntary tech transfer per Clause 22), offer substantial purchase commitments on agriculture and energy, and accept an enforcement framework that is genuinely bilateral rather than unilateral US judgment — while preserving policy space for industrial subsidies and technology development. A deal is close enough that patience and pragmatism are rewarded.
key_factors: China Q1 2019 GDP 6.4% beat expectations; March IP +8.5% (strongest since July 2014); stimulus working
US tariffs cover ~$250B of Chinese exports; structural reform demands touch core development model
Enforcement mechanism agreed in principle (April 10) but sovereignty over implementation still contested
China made 'unprecedented proposals' on forced tech transfer (March 28); Foreign Investment Law in progress
Huawei CFO arrest + DOJ indictments signal technology containment beyond trade
'Some tariffs will stay' even after deal — US retaining leverage (US officials, March 2019)
Two Canadians detained (Dec 10, 2018) as apparent retaliation; limits China's moral high ground

Intensive Washington talks; both sides report progress on text, including enforcement language. No final deal signed.
